strengths: L4Q addresses a relevant NLP deployment problem through a coherent design: quantizing the merged base and LoRA weights during training permits inference without a separate adapter path. Layer-local gradient computation offers a plausible route to memory-efficient QAT.

The evaluation covers seven model configurations spanning 3B–33B parameters, two quantization precisions, commonsense reasoning benchmarks, and MMLU. Results generally favor L4Q among the evaluated quantized methods, with some substantial gains: 3-bit LLaMA-2 7B commonsense accuracy reaches 61.3%, versus 57.6% for QLoRA*.

Actual hardware measurements substantiate practical benefits. Reported 7B training memory is 25.4 GB, close to LoRA’s 25.1 GB and below QAT’s 79.5 GB. Inference measurements also demonstrate benefits from eliminating the separate adapter path.
The initialization, rank, and quantization-group ablations provide useful diagnostic evidence. Detailed task results and mathematical derivations make the contribution easier to assess.
weaknesses: A directly relevant baseline is missing: LoRA fine-tuning followed by merging and PTQ. This would test the claimed advantage over decoupled fine-tuning and quantization while producing the same deployment format. Uniform-quantization variants of QLoRA and LoftQ are explicitly identified, but comparisons do not establish superiority over their original configurations; LoftQ’s near-chance 3-bit MMLU performance also warrants investigation.

Resource comparisons are not consistently controlled. Appendix D uses sequence length 128 specifically for L4Q’s 33B model, versus 2048 otherwise, limiting conclusions from its memory and training-time comparisons. Different training durations are justified mainly through a training-loss curve; matched-context measurements and time to comparable held-out quality would provide stronger evidence.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. The manuscript provides no L4Q implementation or operational pseudocode for the custom backward pass, and omits consequential details including LoRA scaling, microbatch size, gradient accumulation, activation checkpointing, and PTQ calibration settings. Because custom memory management is central to the contribution, these omissions materially weaken confidence in reproducing the efficiency results.

The backward equations require clarification. In Equations 29–30, the elementwise clipping mask must multiply the weight gradient before multiplication by the LoRA matrices. Applying the condition outside those matrix products is dimensionally ambiguous. This may be a notation issue, but the implemented gradient needs to be specified unambiguously.

Many accuracy advantages over the strongest comparator are only a few tenths of a percentage point, without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. Superiority is also not universal: on 3-bit LLaMA-2 13B MMLU 5-shot, L4Q scores 50.0 versus QLoRA*’s 50.6. The promising empirical pattern supports further consideration, but the comparison and reproducibility concerns leave the case for Findings borderline.
